title: Implementation of a Cancer Risk Screening and Management Program in a Concierge Family Medicine Clinic
summary: Transform patient care with AI built for genomics. Nest gives your health system a single platform to launch, coordinate, and scale genomic programs.
body_text: Introduction Based on reported personal and family history, a substantial portion of the population is at increased risk of developing cancer and require additional risk management. Ten percent of all U.S. women are at high risk for breast cancer and at least 4% of the US population is estimated to have an inherited cancer risk. Yet, many are unaware of their risk until diagnosed, reflecting significant gaps in routine screening. This inconsistency in cancer risk assessment underscores the urgent need for systematic risk assessment tools and long-term management strategies in routine care settings. Numerous barriers contribute to the gap in effective cancer risk management. Providers often lack the time needed to collect detailed family histories, educate patients, and stay up-to-date with evolving genetic testing guidelines. Ambiguous eligibility criteria, complex test ordering processes, and limited access to genetic expertise all further complicate matters. Additionally, the steps in this process are usually fragmented rather than integrated into electronic medical records (EMRs), which impedes the efficient identification and management of at-risk individuals. To address these challenges, Ms. Medicine, the largest women's health focused concierge primary care network in the United States, partnered with Nest Genomics to implement Nest. Nest is an EMR-integrated, HIPAA-compliant software platform designed to seamlessly incorporate genetic data into patient care, enabling clinicians and patients to better personalize care and to manage individualized risk. Methods Ahead of their appointment, patients receive email or text invitations and reminders to complete a cancer risk assessment via the Nest patient navigator. Nest evaluates eligibility for genetic testing using national guidelines and specific breast cancer risk models for females. Within the EMR integrated Nest app, clinicians can review and modify the patient's history, genetic testing eligibility, and recommended actions like breast MRI and chemoprevention. Clinicians can choose to order genetic testing, and Nest will send all the required information directly to the lab and return the structured results to the EMR. Nest's clinical decision support then allows clinicians to create a personalized management plan based on the patient's risk and genetic results. Nest will automatically create orders within the EMR tied to actionable steps in the approved care plan and populate the encounter note. The Nest patient navigator helps patients understand their cancer risk and adhere to their care plan. Results Since implemented on January 21st 2024, the comprehensive cancer risk assessment was run on 66 patients at a new Ms. Medicine clinic in Ohio. 78 patients were invited to Nest to complete the risk assessment ahead of their appointment. Seventy opened the invite (90%) and of those, 66 (94%) completed the cancer risk assessment. For patients not invited ahead of visit (n=4) or invited not completed ahead of visit (n=5), a clinician ran the assessment within the Nest app in the EMR during the visit. Three patients (3/66, 5%) received recommendations for both breast MRI and chemoprevention. Thirty three (50%) met genetic testing criteria, of those meeting criteria 16 (48%) had genetic testing ordered. Nest was used to create a personalized care plan for 30 patients and of those 17 (57%) reviewed the care plan when prompted by Nest. Conclusions Implementing the Nest platform in concierge family medicine settings has proven to be a feasible and effective strategy for identifying and improving the management of at-risk individuals. The use of the Nest platform helps providers overcome barriers to cancer risk management and standardizes the process for all patients. The platform and its workflows will continue to be refined based on feedback from participants and clinicians, as well as screening uptake and outcomes. Nest and Ms. Medicine plan to expand to more sites and apply the insights gained from the cancer risk assessment workflow to other specialties, such as cardiology.

title: Dental Adjustment Rate Benchmarks: What's Normal in 2026
body_text: The top dental adjustment rate benchmark for 2026 is the industry-standard 30–45% range for PPO-participating general practices established by Dental Intelligence, Practice by Numbers , and dental consulting groups analyzing more than 10,000 practices nationwide. Metro-area practices in competitive markets can approach or exceed 50%. The average PPO-participating practice writes off 42–45% in contractual discounts before collecting a single dollar, and understanding where your numbers fall against this benchmark is the first step toward knowing whether your PPO contracts are working for you or against you. This guide covers the 2026 dental adjustment rate benchmarks by practice type and specialty, the exact formula for calculating your rate, what drives write-offs higher, how the adjustment rate compares to other key billing metrics, and how to evaluate whether your numbers are working for or against your practice. For most PPO-participating general practices, a dental adjustment rate of 30–45% is the established benchmark for 2026. The number itself is not the problem what matters is whether your net collection rate is near 98% and whether your practice is capturing all the production it's entitled to bill for. The single most reliable indicator of billing health is your net collection rate , not your adjustment rate. Key Takeaways Benchmarks and billing: The typical dental PPO adjustment rate in 2026 is 30–45% of gross production meaning a practice producing $1M writes off $300K–$450K in contractual discounts before collecting a dollar ( Dental Billing Assist ). Adjustment rate and net collection rate measure different things a high adjustment rate is not the same as a billing problem; a low net collection rate is. Track both. Metro-area practices can approach or exceed 40% adjustment rates in the most competitive metro corridors due to more competitive payer markets and lower contracted fee schedules, per dental consulting groups. Warning signs and upstream factors: A contractual adjustment rate consistently above 50% warrants a formal PPO contract review the math may no longer support participation in certain plans. Non-contractual adjustments that exceed your documented policy thresholds are a red flag they signal unauthorized write-offs or billing errors that compound into significant revenue loss. Front desk performance directly impacts net revenue recovery practices that miss 20–35% of inbound calls lose legitimate production that no billing improvement can recover. AI receptionists answering after-hours and overflow calls around the clock adds to the production base that your billing team actually gets to work with. What Is a Dental Adjustment Rate? A dental adjustment rate is the percentage of gross production that a practice writes off as reductions either required by insurance contract terms or made at the practice's discretion. In 2026, contractual adjustments from PPO insurance participation account for the vast majority of write-offs in most dental practices. There are two types of adjustments that make up this rate: Contractual adjustments Required write-offs under your PPO fee schedules. When Delta Dental's contracted rate for a crown is $850 and your full fee is $1,400, the $550 difference is a contractual adjustment. You agreed to accept the discounted rate when you signed the contract. Non-contractual (discretionary) adjustments Write-offs made at your discretion: professional courtesy discounts, billing error corrections, hardship accommodations, and collections settlements. These should be tracked separately. Most practices report a combined adjustment rate that includes both types. When dental consulting groups cite dental adjustment rate benchmarks, they typically refer to the total adjustment rate as a percentage of gross production . Key concept: The dental adjustment rate is the best single measure of your payer mix and PPO discount depth. It does not directly measure billing quality. A practice with 80% PPO patients will show a high adjustment rate and still have an excellent net collection rate because they're collecting nearly everything they're allowed to collect. The net collection rate is the definitive measure of billing performance. How to Calculate Your Dental Adjustment Rate Calculating your adjustment rate uses this formula: Adjustment Rate = (Total Adjustments ÷ Gross Production) × 100 Where: Total Adjustments = all contractual write-offs + non-contractual write-offs for the period Gross Production = total production at full fee before any write-offs Example: A general practice produces $1,200,000 at full UCR fees in a year. Total contractual write-offs from PPO contracts are $480,000. Discretionary adjustments add another $24,000. Adjustment Rate = ($504,000 ÷ $1,200,000) × 100 = 42% This means 42 cents of every dollar produced is written off before billing. The practice's adjusted production the amount actually collectible is $696,000. Separate your adjustment types in your practice management software. Most PMS platforms including Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental, Denticon, and Curve Dental allow you to code contractual and non-contractual adjustments differently. See our guide to OpenDental optimization for step-by-step adjustment code setup. This separation lets you evaluate your PPO participation decisions independent of front desk discretionary write-offs. How We Evaluated These Benchmarks Our analysis draws from the ADA Health Policy Institute's practice economics surveys, data published by Dental Intelligence across more than 10,000 dental practices, revenue cycle reports from dental billing specialist firms, and dental consulting groups including Practice by Numbers and the Dental Group Practice Association. We scored dental adjustment rate benchmarks across five dimensions: Payer mix weight adjustment rates normalized by PPO patient percentage Market geography metro vs. suburban vs. rural contracted fee schedule variation Practice scale solo vs. group vs. DSO benchmark ranges Specialty type general dentistry, orthodontics, oral surgery, pediatric, periodontics Write-off classification contractual vs. non-contractual adjustment separation Based on our analysis, the single most reliable predictor of dental practice financial health is not the adjustment rate itself, but the relationship between adjustment rate and net collection rate. Practices achieving 98%+ net collection with 42–45% adjustment rates consistently outperform practices at 85–90% net collection with 30% adjustment rates because a disciplined adjustment rate without equally disciplined collections still leaves revenue on the table. Dental Adjustment Rate Benchmarks for 2026 Dental adjustment rate benchmarks in 2026 range from 30–45% of gross production for PPO-participating general practices, with most active-PPO practices averaging 42–45% . Fee-for-service and PPO-lite practices typically fall below 20%, while metro-area heavy-PPO practices frequently exceed 50%. The benchmark range varies by specialty, market geography, and payer mix. The following benchmark ranges represent typical performance for general dental practices in 2026, based on analysis from dental practice consulting groups and published industry data : Adjustment Rate Benchmarks Adjustment Rate What It Signals Under 20% Low PPO mix; primarily fee-for-service or Medicaid 20–30% Moderate PPO participation; selective plan mix 30–40% Typical range for general practices with active PPO participation 40–50% Heavy PPO participation; common in competitive markets Above 50% High-volume PPO; review individual plan profitability Source: BoomCloud/Dental Intelligence benchmark data The most common dental adjustment rate benchmark for general practices in 2026 is 30–45%. Data cited by dental consulting groups from Dental Intelligence suggests the average PPO adjustment rate across general practices is 42–45% , meaning the average PPO-participating practice writes off nearly half of gross production before collecting any revenue. What "normal" really means: The dental adjustment rate benchmark of 42% is not inherently problematic it depends entirely on what your net collection rate looks like after that write-off. A practice writing off a moderately high share but collecting nearly all of their allowed charges is performing extremely well. A practice writing off 35% but collecting only 88% has a genuine billing problem despite the lower adjustment rate. The adjustment rate benchmark alone never tells the complete story. Benchmarks by Practice Type and Specialty Adjustment rates vary significantly by specialty, insurance mix, and market geography: Typical Adjustment Rates by Practice Type Practice Type Typical Adjustment Rate Notes General dentistry (heavy PPO) 40–50% Most common profile General dentistry (moderate PPO) 30–40% Selective plan participation Fee-for-service / PPO-lite 5–20% Primarily patient-pay Pediatric dentistry 35–50% High Medicaid and PPO mix Orthodontics 20–35% More private-pay; fewer PPO plans Oral surgery 30–45% Mixed PPO and medical billing Periodontics 30–42% PPO and medical cross-billing DSOs (multi-location groups) 38–48% Higher volume softens impact General dentistry data: BoomCloud/Dental Intelligence . Specialty adjustment rate ranges are editorial estimates based on typical payer mix and are not drawn from published survey data. Geographic variation matters. In competitive metro markets major urban centers where multiple PPO networks compete aggressively contracted fee schedules are often significantly lower than in suburban or rural markets. Practices in high-cost metros typically see adjustment rates toward the higher end of the 30–45% range, with some consultants reporting rates that push even higher in particularly competitive areas, according to dental industry consultants. For DSOs and multi-location groups, the dental revenue cycle management challenges look different at scale adjustment rates aggregate across locations with varied payer mixes, requiring centralized reporting to get an accurate picture. What Drives Your Adjustment Rate Up? Several factors push adjustment rates higher. Understanding which factors are controllable versus structural helps prioritize where to focus: Structural factors (harder to change quickly): PPO contract fee schedules The discount depth varies by plan. Some major carriers reimburse at 70–80% of usual fees; others reimburse at 50–60%, per ADA Health Policy Institute analysis and PPO negotiation specialists. Participating in lower-reimbursing plans raises your aggregate adjustment rate. Payer mix The more PPO patients in your chair, the higher the aggregate write-off percentage. Market competition More dental offices per capita generally means insurance companies negotiate lower contracted rates. Fee schedule stagnation PPO fee schedules at some major carriers have not updated in years, while practice costs have risen, effectively increasing the real discount depth year over year. According to the ADA Health Policy Institute , dental practice revenues grew just 1.4% while expenses grew 4.9% over a recent five-year period meaning the same contracted fee writes off a larger real-dollar share of a practice's overhead every year. Fee schedule stagnation is the leading cause of rising adjustment rates at practices that haven't proactively requested renegotiation. Structural factors explain why two identical practices in different cities can show a 10–15 percentage point difference in adjustment rates with neither one having a better billing operation than the other. Controllable factors (addressable now): Uncoded discretionary adjustments Courtesy discounts applied inconsistently by front desk staff add to non-contractual adjustments without oversight. Adjustment posting errors Incorrect write-off codes applied during EOB posting can inflate adjustment totals or misclassify contractual discounts as discretionary ones. Failure to renegotiate Many practices accept initial PPO fee schedules without attempting renegotiation. Fee schedules can often be improved meaningfully through formal requests, particularly for specialists or high-volume practices. Participation in marginal plans Some practices participate in every available PPO out of concern for patient volume, including plans that reimburse well below sustainable margins. Controllable factors are where practice management makes the most difference. Addressing discretionary write-offs and posting errors alone can reduce a practice's effective adjustment rate by 2–5 percentage points. Pro Tip: Run an adjustment report segmented by insurance plan quarterly. If a specific carrier shows an adjustment rate significantly above your practice average, that plan warrants a profitability analysis not just a look at visit volume. Note that Delta Dental, Cigna Dental, MetLife Dental, United Concordia, Ameritas, and Guardian Dental are among the largest PPO networks by patient volume, and each reimburses at different discount depths so a single carrier can shift a practice's blended adjustment rate by 3–8 percentage points depending on participation depth. According to ADA surveys , approximately 35% of dentists report planning to drop at least one PPO network within 24 months and the leading driver is adjustment rates that no longer cover overhead at the plan's contracted fee schedule. Knowing your per-plan adjustment rate against the benchmark is the foundation of any PPO exit decision. Adjustment Rate vs. Net Collection Rate These two metrics measure completely different things, and confusing them is one of the most common revenue cycle errors in dental practice management. Revenue Cycle Metrics Comparison Metric What It Measures Benchmark Adjustment Rate How much is written off before billing 30–45% for PPO-heavy practices Net Collection Rate How much of allowable charges you collect 98%+ for top performers Gross Collection Rate Total payments ÷ total production (distorted by payer mix) Not a reliable KPI Net collection rate benchmark: Dentx , Dental Billing Assist . A practice with a moderately high adjustment rate and a near-perfect net collection rate is doing everything right. The high adjustment rate reflects their insurance mix not a billing failure. A practice with a 30% adjustment rate and a 91% net collection rate has a genuine problem. Despite lower PPO participation, they're failing to collect nearly 10% of their allowable charges through claim denials, patient balance failures, or write-off errors. Focus improvement efforts on net collection rate, not adjustment rate. Your adjustment rate is largely determined by your insurance contracts. Your net collection rate is determined by your processes and it is fully controllable. The most common mistake in dental revenue cycle benchmarking is treating a high adjustment rate as a billing failure. It is not. The adjustment rate is a structural feature of your payer mix; the net collection rate is the performance indicator that actually measures whether your team is doing its job. How to Manage Your Contractual Adjustment Rate Managing adjustment rates is about making strategic decisions around PPO participation, not eliminating write-offs entirely. Key actions: Evaluate PPO plan profitability individually: Run a per-plan analysis: production, write-offs, and net collections by carrier Calculate your effective hourly rate for each plan after write-offs Flag any plan where the effective rate falls below your target Pursue fee schedule renegotiation: Formal renegotiation requests succeed more often than practices expect, particularly when backed by production volume data Use your UCR fee update (typically annual) as a trigger to request increases from carriers Specialists periodontists, oral surgeons, endodontists often have more leverage than general dentists Standardize discretionary adjustment policies: Define written policies for when courtesy adjustments are permitted Require manager approval for write-offs above a defined threshold Track non-contractual adjustments as a percentage of production monthly and flag any amount that appears inconsistent with your documented discount policies Audit your EOB posting process for accuracy: Incorrect adjustment codes during posting inflate your reported adjustment rate EOB adjustment errors are more common than most practices realize a meaningful share of manual EOB postings can contain write-off errors The most impactful fee renegotiation strategy is to request increases immediately after your annual UCR fee update, backed by production volume data. This single action can reduce your effective adjustment rate by 3–8 percentage points over 12–24 months at carriers with negotiable schedules. For solo practices, a structured approach to managing AR days is essential alongside adjustment rate monitoring the two metrics work together to reveal the full health of your revenue cycle. How Front Desk Efficiency Affects Revenue Recovery One critical factor many dental practices overlook: your adjustment rate only matters for the production you actually capture. Missed calls represent production that never enters your revenue cycle at all. Dental practices miss 20–35% of inbound calls during business hours, according to industry estimates . Each missed call from a new patient represents hundreds of dollars in same-visit production and thousands in lifetime patient value. Comparing PPO Plans by Adjustment Rate ROI Per-plan ROI comparison is the most actionable use of dental adjustment rate benchmarks more impactful than overall practice-level comparisons. A per-plan ROI analysis is the most effective method for identifying which PPO contracts to renegotiate or exit. Common Mistakes in Adjustment Rate Tracking Mixing contractual and non-contractual adjustments in a single bucket. When these are lumped together, you can't diagnose whether your adjustment rate is driven by your PPO contracts (expected) or by discretionary write-off behavior (controllable). Using gross collection rate as a proxy for billing performance. Gross collection rate is distorted by payer mix. A 75% gross collection rate at a heavy-PPO practice may reflect a 97% net collection rate meaning excellent billing performance. Track net collection rate instead. Benchmarking against the wrong peer group. A solo general practice in a suburban market should not benchmark against a DSO in a major metro. Adjustment rates vary dramatically by market, specialty, and scale. Ignoring fee schedule update timing. PPO fee schedules typically update on an annual cycle, but the effective write-off depth increases between updates as your UCR fees rise. Failing to request fee schedule updates consistently allows adjustment rates to creep upward year over year. Failing to audit write-offs at the individual plan level. Aggregate adjustment rate analysis hides individual plan performance. Frequently Asked Questions What is a normal dental adjustment rate in 2026? A normal dental adjustment rate for a PPO-participating general practice in 2026 is typically 30–45% of gross production . Practices with heavy PPO participation or in competitive metro markets frequently see rates of 42–45%, while practices with a more selective insurance mix may run 25–35%. Fee-for-service practices may see rates under 20%. What sets a contractual adjustment apart from a write-off? A contractual adjustment is a pre-agreed discount under a PPO contract you must write off the difference between your UCR fee and the contracted rate. A write-off (in the context of bad debt) refers to uncollectible patient balances removed from receivables. Contractual adjustments are expected and budgeted; bad-debt write-offs signal a collection problem. Does a high adjustment rate mean I have a billing problem? No. A high adjustment rate reflects your insurance mix how many PPO patients you see and how deeply your contracted fee schedules discount your full fees. A billing problem shows up in your net collection rate , not your adjustment rate. A practice with a moderately high adjustment rate and a near-perfect net collection rate is performing exceptionally well. How do I know if my PPO adjustment rate is too high? The question to ask is not whether your adjustment rate exceeds a benchmark, but whether the net production per hour from each PPO plan is sustainable. Specialists and high-volume practices tend to have the most leverage. Many practices update their UCR fees annually and use that event to request corresponding increases from insurance carriers. How does missing calls affect my dental revenue cycle? Missed calls represent production that never enters your revenue cycle. PPO fee schedules at major carriers typically update infrequently, while practice costs and UCR fees rise annually. The effective discount depth grows even without any change to your plan participation meaning the same PPO contracts write off a larger share of a higher fee, year over year. A rising adjustment rate warrants an annual fee schedule renegotiation request, not quiet acceptance. How do I know when to drop a PPO plan entirely? When the net production per hour after contractual write-offs falls below your target effective rate typically calculated against your overhead per hour plus acceptable margin the plan is costing you money. Volume matters too: a lower-reimbursing plan may still be worth keeping if it reliably fills otherwise open chair time. Run a per-plan profitability analysis in your practice management software to make this call with data, not gut feel. What percentage of dental production should be written off? For a PPO-participating general practice, contractual adjustments of 30–45% of gross production are normal and expected. Non-contractual (discretionary) adjustments courtesy discounts, billing error corrections should be tracked monthly, and any amount inconsistent with your documented discount policies signals a management or audit issue that warrants immediate review. How do I negotiate my PPO fee schedule to cut write-offs? Request a fee schedule review directly from the insurance carrier's provider relations department, backed by production volume data, clean claims history, and a formal written request. The best timing is immediately after your annual UCR fee update. Most major carriers allow renegotiation every 12–24 months. High-volume practices and specialists typically have the most leverage, and persistence across multiple touchpoints is often required. What causes dental adjustment rates to rise year over year? The most common cause is fee schedule stagnation PPO contracted rates that do not update while practice costs and UCR fees rise annually. The same contracted rate becomes a larger real-dollar write-off each year. Expanding PPO participation, adding lower-reimbursing plans, and entering more competitive markets also push adjustment rates higher over time. Requesting annual fee schedule increases from carriers is the primary defense. Final Verdict Your adjustment rate benchmark means different things depending on your practice profile. Here is how to read yours in context. Low to moderate adjustment rates: Under 30%: Your PPO mix is selective. If your schedule stays full, this is a financial advantage. If you are seeing open chair time, a targeted expansion of select PPO plans may increase volume without crossing unsustainable write-off levels. 30–45%: Normal range for a PPO-participating general practice. The right question is your net collection rate if it is at 98% or above, your revenue cycle is working correctly despite the write-offs. High adjustment rates that need attention: 45–50%: Heavy PPO participation. Run a per-plan profitability analysis to identify which carriers are pulling your effective hourly rate below target. Above 50%: A formal PPO contract review is warranted. title: RevPAR Explained: What It Is and How to Calculate It
summary: What is RevPAR, and why does it mislead hotel owners. Learn to calculate it correctly and stop letting invisible revenue gaps drain your property.
body_text: RevPAR tells you the score, not how the game was played. Here is what the industry's default room metric actually measures, where it goes blind, and why that gap costs operators more than they think. RevPAR, short for Revenue per Available Room , is the hospitality industry's most widely tracked room-level performance metric. Most hospitality business owners think that if their RevPAR isn't moving, they need to adjust their pricing strategy or their channel mix, those are the two levers they control. But that assumption skips past what RevPAR actually measures, and more importantly, where it stops measuring, and for operators managing lean portfolios, that gap is the difference between diagnosing a revenue problem and missing it entirely. See our AI for hospitality for how this works in practice. RevPAR (Revenue per Available Room) is a critical hospitality KPI that measures a property's ability to fill its rooms at an average rate across a given period. A 100-room hotel generating $8,000 in room revenue on a single night has a RevPAR of $80, whether 80 rooms were occupied or 100. The denominator is always total available rooms, not just the ones that sold. That distinction matters more than most operators realize. The metric captures the relationship between two inputs: how many rooms you sold and at what price. Strong occupancy with a weak rate produces a low RevPAR. A high rate with too many empty rooms produces the same result. RevPAR surfaces both failure modes in one number, which is exactly why it became the default room-revenue benchmark across the industry. Industry research widely regards RevPAR as the hospitality industry's default room-revenue benchmark because it requires minimal inputs and translates instantly across property types and market sizes. RevPAR only counts revenue that completed a booking cycle. It has no visibility into the inquiry that went unanswered at 1am, the quote that expired before a follow-up landed, or the guest who booked somewhere else by morning. That lost revenue never enters the calculation. Key takeaways RevPAR is Revenue per Available Room, it tells you how much room revenue your available inventory generated, nothing more and nothing less. Two formulas build the same number: ADR multiplied by occupancy rate, or total room revenue divided by rooms available, and the split between those inputs matters more than the headline figure. A rising RevPAR can mask a broken operation: high ADR with cratering occupancy and high occupancy with suppressed rates both produce identical RevPAR scores. RevPAR ignores ancillary revenue, distribution costs, and labor, which is why GOPPAR and TRevPAR exist and why profitable operators track all three. Inquiry response speed is a revenue variable, not a courtesy one, leads that go unanswered past the first few minutes convert at a fraction of the rate of leads touched immediately. The gap between a strong RevPAR and your actual revenue potential is mostly an execution problem, not a pricing problem, and it widens every night your front desk goes dark. Conduit's AI-powered guest communication tools keep that gap from compounding by handling booking inquiries around the clock, so the 1am lead doesn't become someone else's confirmed reservation. How Do You Calculate RevPAR? (Both Formulas, With Examples) Pick up a STR/CoStar data release and you will find RevPAR printed as a single, tidy number. What you will not find is any indication of how that number was built, or whether the inputs holding it up are healthy. The core diagnostic problem is this: RevPAR's dual-formula construction , ADR × Occupancy, makes it mathematically impossible to diagnose whether a plateau is a pricing failure or a fill-rate failure, because the same flat RevPAR number can be produced by a dozen different ADR/occupancy combinations; operators who treat a stable RevPAR as a stable strategy are actually reading a single output and hallucinating a cause. For operators trying to diagnose a plateau, knowing which formula to run first is the difference between spotting the real problem and chasing the wrong fix. There is a subtler trap layered on top of this one. A market can post strong RevPAR growth year-over-year and still sit well below the national average in absolute RevPAR terms. That gap matters because operators who benchmark only against their own prior performance can mistake momentum for market parity. Raw RevPAR values are genuinely misleading without the right context, and building a business that does not depend entirely on owner-level interpretation of every metric is exactly what separates scalable STR operations from ones that stall. Both formulas below are tools for building that context systematically. Formula 1 - Total Revenue Divided by Available Rooms RevPAR = Total Room Revenue / Total Available Rooms. A property collects $8,000 in room revenue across 100 available rooms on a given night; RevPAR is $80. Your property management system almost certainly runs this version automatically, which is exactly why it gets used without much thought. It tells you only what the score was, not how the game was played. A revenue dip looks identical whether it came from a rate problem or a fill-rate problem, and the formula gives you no way to tell them apart. Formula 2 - ADR Times Occupancy Rate RevPAR = Average Daily Rate (ADR) × Occupancy Rate. This is the diagnostic version. Take the same 100-room night: if ADR was $160 and occupancy was 50%, RevPAR is $80. If ADR was $100 and occupancy was 80%, RevPAR is also $80. Same score, completely different operational story. The first property has a fill-rate problem; the second has a pricing problem. Formula 2 makes that split visible in one calculation, and it is the split that determines which lever an operator should pull next. Worked Example - Running Both Formulas on the Same Night S. 70. 70. The outputs match exactly. Formula 2 immediately shows that roughly 37 rooms sat empty that night and that ADR is doing most of the heavy lifting. 70 but your occupancy is 75% rather than 63%, your ADR is actually lagging the benchmark, a pricing problem, not a fill-rate win. That is the kind of diagnosis a single RevPAR headline number will never surface on its own. Operators managing multiple properties face a compounding version of this challenge: they need that two-formula diagnostic running consistently across every unit, not just the one they happen to be watching. Conduit's AI Agents and Workflows are built for exactly that operating reality, most beneficial when the business has recurring, predictable guest touchpoints that currently require manual staff action and when it receives a high volume of repetitive guest or customer messages. By handling guest communications automatically before, during, and after a stay, the platform frees the operations team to focus on revenue diagnostics rather than inbox triage. The goal is a systemized, scalable business that does not depend entirely on owner involvement in every conversation, or every formula check. Why Does RevPAR Matter: and What a Good RevPAR Number Actually Signals Watching your RevPAR climb month over month feels like confirmation that the revenue strategy is working. But RevPAR is better understood as a diagnostic lens than a destination metric. The split between ADR and occupancy sitting underneath it tells you far more than the headline figure ever will. RevPAR Collapses Two Variables into One Signal, and That Is Exactly Its Power RevPAR matters because it answers a question that neither occupancy nor ADR can answer alone: how effectively are you converting your available room inventory into actual revenue? A property running 95% occupancy sounds impressive until you learn the ADR is $80. A property with a $220 ADR sounds equally strong until occupancy sits at 45%. RevPAR collapses both inputs into one comparable figure, giving operators a single, honest read on room-level revenue performance across dates, seasons, and properties. For operators managing multiple properties simultaneously, that single figure also becomes a cross-portfolio signal, one place to spot which assets are underperforming before the monthly P&L confirms it. Building a systemized, scalable operation that does not depend entirely on owner involvement means the RevPAR read has to be legible to your operations team, not just to you. Ai are designed to close, by centralizing the conversation layer across properties so the operations team has full visibility without the owner being in every thread. The Two Failure Modes RevPAR Surfaces That Occupancy and ADR Hide Individually The same RevPAR number can hide opposite problems. High occupancy with a weak ADR means you filled the rooms but priced them too low, leaving margin on the table. High ADR with low occupancy means the rate is strong but demand is not converting, and empty rooms generate zero revenue regardless of what they were listed at. hotel occupancy fell 2.5% year-over-year while ADR rose only 0.4%, two variables moving in opposite directions simultaneously. Watching either metric in isolation that month would have given operators an incomplete, potentially misleading picture of where the real pressure was coming from. What makes this failure mode especially costly at scale is that the diagnostic conversation, the back-and-forth between owner, operations lead, and front-desk staff trying to figure out why conversion is soft, consumes hours that a systemized operation cannot afford to spend reactively. When the operations or support team is already stretched monitoring guest communications across multiple platforms, adding a performance-triage loop on top of it compounds the drag. Why a Rising RevPAR Can Still Mean Falling Profit - Distribution Costs Explained Here is the synthesis that most RevPAR discussions never surface explicitly: OTA-driven RevPAR growth is a self-canceling strategy, because the same channel activity that lifts RevPAR above the line simultaneously locks in 15–25% commission costs below it. Because RevPAR does not net out distribution expenses, operators using it as their primary health signal will systematically over-invest in the channel mix that is quietly destroying their NOI, discovering the damage only in quarterly P&L statements, long after the high-commission bookings have checked out. markets: properties in the same metro can show similar RevPAR figures while sitting on dramatically different net operating outcomes depending on their channel mix. The number at the top of the report does not tell you which properties are building equity and which are funding OTA growth at their own expense. How the RevPAR Index Turns a Raw Number into a Competitive Verdict The RevPAR Index , also called the Revenue Generation Index (RGI) , solves the relativity problem directly. An RGI of 100 means your property is capturing exactly its fair share of RevPAR relative to your defined competitive set. Above 100, you are outperforming the set; below 100, the competitive set is taking share you should be capturing. Tracking RGI alongside raw STR/CoStar benchmarks is what turns a single headline figure into an actionable competitive verdict, and it is the kind of ongoing monitoring that scales cleanly when the operational layer underneath it is already systemized rather than owner-dependent. The Limitations of RevPAR - What the Number Can't See RevPAR is useful until the moment you need to know whether your property is actually making money, and that moment arrives faster than most operators expect. The metric captures room revenue per available room but goes silent on everything that happens between a booking and a bank deposit, which means a rising RevPAR can carry genuine financial risk dressed up as good news. The sub-sections below break down exactly where that silence lives and why the layers RevPAR ignores are the same layers where smarter communication execution tends to move the needle most. A Higher RevPAR Does Not Mean Higher Profit Most hospitality business owners think that if their RevPAR isn't moving, they need to adjust their pricing strategy or their channel mix, those are the two levers they control. But healthy RevPAR numbers can be the most expensive kind of false confidence an operator carries into a Monday morning ownership call. The metric tells you how much room revenue your property generated per available room, but it says nothing about how much of that revenue actually survived the journey from booking to bank account. Understanding where RevPAR goes quiet is the difference between managing a dashboard and managing a business. The deeper problem is structural, not incidental. TRevPAR and GOPPAR are not merely "more complete" versions of RevPAR, they reveal that the ancillary and cost layers RevPAR ignores are precisely where AI-driven guest communication generates its highest-leverage revenue impact, meaning operators benchmarking only RevPAR are measuring the one dimension of their business least sensitive to communication execution. An increase in RevPAR does not necessarily mean higher profits. Consider a property that raises its Average Daily Rate by 15 percent. RevPAR climbs, the dashboard looks strong, and the ownership report goes out with a green arrow. But if filling those rooms required last-minute staff overtime and the bulk of new bookings came through OTA channels, net operating income can land flat or lower than the month before. RevPAR registered the win. The profit-and-loss statement told a different story. The metric captures top-line room revenue, not what remains after the costs that made that revenue possible. Operators who benchmark success on RevPAR alone are measuring the output of a process whose inputs are quietly working against them. RevPAR Is Blind to Operating Costs, Labor, OTA Commissions, and the Margin Illusion RevPAR does not account for operating costs, and two cost lines in particular make that silence expensive. Labor consistently represents one of the largest cost categories in hospitality operations. When RevPAR rises because a property pushed hard to fill rooms through aggressive staffing or extended service hours, the headline number improves while the margin underneath compresses. OTA commissions compound the problem. According to EHL Insights , OTAs typically charge hotels commission rates of 15 to 25 percent per booking . That cost sits entirely beneath the RevPAR line. Operators who shift channel mix toward OTAs to lift occupancy may be trading margin for the appearance of momentum. Every direct booking captured instead of an OTA referral improves GOPPAR without moving RevPAR at all, a gain that standard benchmarking will never surface. This is where the structural nature of the problem becomes most visible. The cost of a booking is not just the commission line; it includes the staff time spent answering pre-booking inquiries, managing follow-up messages across multiple platforms, and manually executing touchpoints after check-in. And nowhere is that blind spot more consequential than in how response speed compounds invisibly into revenue outcomes: inquiry response speed is not a hospitality courtesy variable but a compounding revenue multiplier. Hotels that respond to inquiries within five minutes are far more likely to convert that lead, and slow responders face algorithmic distribution penalties from OTA platforms that suppress future demand exposure. That same logic applies to how operators read performance metrics. Two properties can post identical RevPAR figures while sitting at completely different financial positions: one profitable, one quietly bleeding margin through untracked ancillary revenue and rising operating costs. That gap is exactly what TRevPAR and GOPPAR are built to surface. TRevPAR (Total Revenue per Available Room) adds every dollar the property earns beyond the room rate, food and beverage, spa, parking, paid early check-ins, into a single per-room figure. GOPPAR (Gross Operating Profit per Available Room) goes further, subtracting operating expenses to show what the property actually keeps. Together, they give operators a complete financial picture that RevPAR alone will never deliver. 1. TRevPAR - Best for Full-Service Hotels with Multiple Revenue Streams TRevPAR is the right metric when a meaningful share of guest spending happens outside the room. At full-service hotels and resorts, ancillary revenue, F&B, spa, activities, and paid add-ons, routinely represents a significant portion of total property revenue, as broader industry trends consistently show. A boutique hotel with a rooftop bar could show flat RevPAR while TRevPAR climbs 18%, because the real revenue driver was the bar, a pattern that holds across the market, where ancillary revenue routinely represents a significant share of full-service property totals. GOPPAR - Best for Ownership and Asset Management Decision-Making GOPPAR is the metric ownership groups and asset managers reach for when the conversation shifts from revenue to returns. By folding operating expenses into the calculation, it connects directly to NOI and investor reporting in a way RevPAR and TRevPAR cannot. RevPAR vs. GOPPAR as Strategic Metrics - When to Use Each Based on Management Goals Choosing between RevPAR and GOPPAR depends on your strategic lens: RevPAR suits short-term pricing and occupancy decisions, while GOPPAR aligns with long-term profitability and investor reporting. Research published in the Journal of Revenue and Pricing Management confirms neither metric is universally superior, context determines fit. How to Improve RevPAR - Including the Operational Lever Most Operators Ignore Pricing strategy gets most of the attention when RevPAR stalls. The Standard RevPAR Improvement Playbook Dynamic pricing, demand forecasting, channel mix optimization, and length-of-stay controls form the core of most hotel revenue strategies. Studies on dynamic pricing consistently show meaningful RevPAR lift when rates respond to real-time demand signals rather than static seasonal schedules. Shifting direct booking share away from high-commission OTA channels compounds that gain by improving net revenue per booking. These are legitimate, well-documented levers, and operators who haven't optimized them should start there. Where Rate Optimization Hits Its Ceiling Pricing tools optimize for a room's rate potential, not its conversion probability. Once your rates are competitive and your channel mix is clean, you've set the ceiling. How close you get to that ceiling depends on execution: specifically, whether every inquiry actually converts into a confirmed booking. A room priced perfectly at 11pm that goes unbooked because no one answered a 1am message is a RevPAR suppressor no dynamic pricing tool can see, measure, or fix. Platform algorithms compound the problem: slow responders lose listing visibility, meaning communication speed affects demand exposure, not just conversion rate. RevPAR and Operational Execution - What Pricing Tools Cannot Fix The honest trade-off: this approach requires upfront investment in building a reliable AI knowledge base , and it works best for operators handling consistent inquiry volume across multiple units or time zones. A single-property owner with low overnight inquiry volume may see less immediate impact. Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between ADR and RevPAR? ADR (Average Daily Rate) measures only the average price of rooms that actually sold, while RevPAR divides total room revenue by all available rooms, including the ones that went unsold. That means RevPAR captures both your pricing performance and your fill rate in a single number, while ADR tells you nothing about how many rooms sat empty. What does RevPAR actually tell you about your property's performance? RevPAR tells you how effectively you are converting your total available room inventory into actual revenue across a given period. When you break it into its two inputs, ADR and occupancy, it also reveals which of the two is the source of any underperformance: a fill-rate problem or a pricing problem, which determines which lever you should pull next. Can RevPAR go up while my actual profit goes down? Yes. If rooms are filled through OTA channels, commissions of 15 to 25 percent per booking sit entirely beneath the RevPAR line, so a rising RevPAR can coincide with compressed net operating income. Similarly, if filling rooms required last-minute staff overtime, the headline number improves while the margin underneath it does not, RevPAR captures top-line room revenue, not what survives after the costs that made that revenue possible. What are the main limitations of using RevPAR as your primary performance metric? RevPAR has three core blind spots: it cannot distinguish between a pricing failure and a fill-rate failure without being broken into its ADR and occupancy components; it is invisible to operating costs like labor and OTA commissions that directly affect profit; and it excludes all non-room revenue, meaning ancillary income streams never enter the calculation. Metrics like GOPPAR and TRevPAR exist precisely because they capture the cost and total-revenue layers that RevPAR ignores. Is there a single RevPAR number that counts as 'good'? There is no universal threshold, because a raw RevPAR number is genuinely misleading without context. The post points to the RevPAR Index (also called the Revenue Generation Index, or RGI) as the more meaningful benchmark: an RGI of 100 means your property is capturing exactly its fair share relative to your competitive set, above 100 means you are outperforming it, and below 100 means the competitive set is taking share you should be capturing.
